title: Day 45 · Week 6, Day 3 — Parents: your head — the father nobody screens, the hormone that is already falling, and the treatment with a thousand trials behind it
summary: The third Parents episode, and the one about the father. Your baby is 5–7 mm at the start of Carnegie stage 14: lens pits sinking into the sides of the head, arm buds lengthening, the brain half again as large as yesterday. The shape of the thing: in 312 first-time fathers followed from 23 weeks to one year, symptom levels were highest in pregnancy (Condon 2004); stress peaks at the birth, driven by role restriction and being an onlooker (Philpott 2017). The numbers: paternal depression 8.4% across 74 studies and 41,480 men (Cameron 2016), 13.6% in the first trimester (Rao 2020), 10.4% overall (Paulson & Bazemore 2010); paternal anxiety 4.1–16% in pregnancy and 2.4–18% postnatally (Leach 2016) against 18.2% first-trimester anxiety symptoms in mothers (Dennis 2017); a preconception history of major depression carrying 6× the odds of perinatal depression and 4× of anxiety (Lowrie 2022); resident fathers' depressive symptoms rising 68% across the first five years of fatherhood in 10,623 men (Garfield 2014). The body: testosterone falling a median 26% (waking) and 34% (evening) in 624 men who became fathers, lowest in those doing 3+ hours of daily care (Gettler 2011); significant declines in testosterone and estradiol across pregnancy in 29 expectant fathers (Edelstein 2015); low testosterone going with paternal depression but high testosterone with maternal depression, aggression and fathering stress in 149 couples (Saxbe 2017) — so don't 'fix' it; BMI drifting up with fatherhood (Garfield 2016); sleep down 13 minutes for men versus 62 for women, unrecovered at six years (Richter 2019). The gap: ACOG CO 757 screens her, not you; fathers feel like bystanders across 22 qualitative studies (Baldwin 2018). The tools: the EPDS with a men's cut-off of 5/6 (Matthey 2001, 208 fathers) and the GAD-7 at 10 (Spitzer 2006; sensitivity 89%, specificity 82%). What works: father-specific trials are thin (11 studies; Rominov 2016); counselling cuts perinatal depression onset 39% in at-risk pregnant women (O'Connor 2019, USPSTF) and psychosocial support cuts postpartum depression 22% (Cochrane 2013); and physical activity, in 97 reviews, 1,039 trials and 128,119 people, has medium effects on depression (−0.43), anxiety (−0.42) and distress (−0.60), larger at higher intensity (Singh 2023), with Cochrane's exercise-for-depression review agreeing. Showing up is, on this evidence, also what helps you.
action: Tonight, fifteen minutes, alone first: find the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale and the GAD-7, take both, and write the two numbers and the date in the pregnancy file under your partner's entry from the Day 40 sheet. Six or more on the Edinburgh (the men's cut-off) or ten or more on the GAD-7 means you book an appointment with your own doctor this week and say 'my partner's six weeks pregnant and I scored above the line on a screen.' If you have had a depression before, book it anyway. Either way, put three thirty-minute exercise sessions in your own calendar for the next seven days and make one of them her walk. Then tell one person — your partner or a friend — the number you got.
